title_en: Removal of the Stigma Against Women
translation:
Pointing to the seven wealthy thieves, the Samagam said that all of them mix among us in Vishnu bhakti (devotion to Lord Vishnu) only so that they may afterward lead us down to their own level — they are thieves of Vishnu bhakti. They are the greatest of disguises, like one who hides his face in a shawl so as not to reveal his true nature; in the same way they smother our activity of Vishnu bhakti — they are guerrilla, hidden enemies. Only when one is rid of these things can Vishnu bhakti be attained.

Removal of the Stigma Against Women

Nishkarmi (freed-from-ritual-obligation) women — the fault-removal of women, among sages who themselves performed ritual works: Maharaj Jivandasji, in Samvat 1688, revealed the Uda Vaishnav (rite-free devotee) path, free of ritualism. But he could not bear that, in the name of the ritual custom of rajasvala dharma (the rule governing a woman's monthly period) then prevalent among women, women were dishonored and addressed as chandali (outcaste woman), brahma-hatyarini (killer of a brahmin), dhoban (washerwoman) and the like, being treated as untouchable. In propagating the Uda dharma, when he removed the faults of the ritualistic observances current in society — japa (chanting), tapa (austerity), pilgrimage, vows, and so on — he gave women the right to wear the tilak and hold the tulsi, and he abolished the practices of dowry, paithan (bride-price), and the buying and selling of brides or grooms. He also put an end to the cruelties inflicted on women in after-death rites — beating the chest in mourning (chhajiya), formal mourning, wearing black clothes, shaving the hair, and so forth — rules that continue in our society to this day. But there was one still greater blemish: women were treated with contempt at the time of menstruation and were dishonored by being regarded as untouchable. Maharaj Jivanji could not bear this blemish, so among all the revolutions he brought about in the devotee community through the Samagam, one great revolution was this: on a day in Samvat 1734 he issued a Proclamation that a fortunate man performs Vishnu bhakti — but, on the other side, 'I remove the ritual obligation (karma) from women.' Using his own authority to grant them the power and the freedom to act according to their own will, he issued an ordinance that women who are menstruating (rajasvala) should not be scorned as untouchable, declaring, 'I remove the ritual obligation from women. You are to prepare a thal (offering) of one and a quarter ser (a traditional unit of weight) on Sama Pancham (the fifth day of the bright fortnight, this community's counterpart to Rishi Panchami).' Revered Yadunathji Maharaj notes, on the back of leaf (litiyu) no. 27, page 16, that Maharaj Jivanji took upon himself the fault of not observing rajasvala restrictions, and said that the Lord be offered a thal of one and a quarter ser on that fifth day.

To remove the fault ascribed to women for their menstruation, in the Samagam Maharaj Jivanji sought to strengthen his position by citing the example, from the Bhagavat, of the sages' wives.

The Shrimad Bhagavat itself provides the witness and proof that the ritual obligation (karma) of women has been removed. In this episode from the Bhagavat, the sages had forbidden their wives from taking food to Lord Krishna, yet those women went against their husbands' command and took the food to Krishna anyway. This proves that no fault of breaking their husbands' command attached to those women. To show that no fault attaches to breaking a rule that holds one back from a good deed, Narsinh Mehta wrote this hymn (pad):

_Narayan-nu sumaran karta, vare tene tajie re. Mansa vacha karamana, Shri Lakshmivarne bhajie re. Kune tajie kutumbne tajie, tajie ma ne baap re. Bhrat sahit bhaginine tajie, jem taje kanchali saap re. Partham pita Prahlade tajiya, na tajya Hari naam re. Bharath Shatrudhne taji janeta, vahala kidha Shri Ram re. Rishi patnie Shrikrishnaji malva, tajela bharthar re. Tema to kudun kai na padiyun, paami padarath chaar re. Brijnari Vitthalne kaje, ghar taji van chalya re. Bhane Narsaiyo Vrindavanma, Mohan mahalya re._ (Whoever obstructs the remembrance of Narayan should be forsaken, and the Lord of Lakshmi should be worshipped in thought, word and deed. For his sake one gives up clan and family, even mother and father, and brother and sister too, the way a snake sheds its skin without attachment. Prahlad was the first to give up his father in this way, yet he never gave up the Lord's name. Bharat gave up his mother for his brother Shatrughna's sake, but held only Shri Ram dear. The sages' wives gave up their own husbands to go and meet Shri Krishna; nothing false or wrong came of it — rather they attained the four fruits of life. The women of Braj left home for Vitthal's [Krishna's] sake and went into the forest; Narsaiyo says these gopis reveled joyously with Krishna in Vrindavan.)

If anyone obstructs the remembrance of Narayan, that is, of the Lord, he should be forsaken, and one should worship the Lord in every way — in thought, word, and deed. For this one must give up one's lineage and family, and set aside even one's mother and father. Likewise one should give up even a sister along with a brother, the way a snake sheds its skin without any attachment. Prahlad was the very first to give up his father and mother in this way, yet he never gave up the Lord's name. Bharatji gave up his own mother for Shatrughna's sake, but did not give up his beloved Ram. The sages' wives, in order to go and meet Krishna, gave up even their own husbands; nothing evil or improper resulted from this — on the contrary, they attained the four fruits [of life] — dharma, artha, kama, and moksha — along with tilak, tulsi, the company of saints, and the Lord's name. The gopis of Braj left home for the sake of Krishna and went off into the forest. Narsinh Mehta says these gopis then reveled joyously with Krishna in Vrindavan in this way.

Bali gave up his guru Shukracharya; Vibhishan gave up Ravan; Narsinh gave up his caste-community; Mira gave up her husband's family.

_Kantakko sang tyagiyo, kije sat sanga. Mite vikar sharirka, lage Hari ranga. Tat tajyo Prahlad jyun, bharath jyon may. Bhabhishan bhai, parharyo, prabhu bhaye sahay. Pandave Kaurav tajya, Dhruv tajyo raj. Shravane naari taji, saaryo sab kaaj. Rishi patniye rishi tajya, gopijan Ved. Shukdeve maya parhari, paaya Hari bhed. Turak tajya Kabir jyon, Namdev kul reet. Jan Gnani jug parharya, laagi Harisu preet._ (Give up the company of thorns [obstacles], keep the company of the true — then the body's afflictions cease and love for the Lord takes hold. Just as Prahlad gave up his father and Bharat his mother, and Vibhishan forsook his brother, so the Lord became their helper. The Pandavas gave up the Kauravas, Dhruv gave up his kingdom. Shravan gave up marrying, and thereby accomplished all his tasks [of serving his parents]. The sages' wives gave up the sages, and the gopis gave up the Vedic path. Shukdev gave up worldly attachment and found the secret of the Lord. Just as Kabir gave up the Muslim [community's ways], so Namdev gave up his family's custom. The devotee Gnani gave up the world in the same way, and love for the Lord took hold.)

One should give up the company of whatever obstructs one, and keep the company of the true. Only then do the body's distractions cease and attachment to devotion to the Lord take hold — just as Prahlad gave up his father, Bharat gave up his mother, and Vibhishan gave up his brother, and for this the Lord became their helper. The Pandavas gave up the Kauravas. Dhruvji gave up his kingdom. Shravan gave up [marrying] a wife, and thereby gained the merit of serving his mother and father. The sages' wives gave up even the sages themselves, and the gopis gave up even the Vedic path. Shukdevji gave up the greatness of worldly life, and was thereby able to attain the secret essence of the Lord's nature. Just as Kabirji gave up the Muslims [of his own community's customary ways], so too Namdevji gave up the family custom of observing the Ekadashi fast. Following all these examples, the devotee Gnaniji likewise gave up worldliness, and love for devotion to the Lord took hold in him — so says the devotee Das Gnaniji.

The Samagam states that the Bhagavat itself supplies the proof that women's ritual obligation was removed — the 39th verse of the 23rd chapter of the Tenth Canto states:

_Taatatraika vidhruta bharta bhagavantam yatha shrutam, hrudopaguhya vijaho deham karmanu bandhanam._ (139) (One of them was held back by her husband; hearing of the Lord's form as described to her, she embraced Him in her heart and gave up the body bound by karma, and attained Him.)

When the women, having filled their plates with food, were going to the Lord, one woman had been shut in [held back] by her husband; that woman, having heard of the Lord's form as described, embraced Him in her heart and gave up the body bound by karma, and she attained the Lord.

Thus it was the sage who incurred the karmic fault of holding that woman back, for he did not recognize Shri Krishna. In this way no fault of karma attaches to the sages' wives, because they bear the name abala, that is, one without independent power — it was for this reason that the Compassionate Lord partook of the food they brought. Because an abala (woman) is bound only by the bond that ties her behind her husband, she does not generate new karma of her own. Thus for a man, endless karma accumulates without limit — from sacrifice, charity, merit-making, vows, pilgrimage, study, teaching, fire-oblation, accepting gifts, circumambulating the earth, and so on. But for the abala, karma attaches to her only if she breaks even a single word of her husband and thereby forsakes her wifely devotion (pativratapanu); so long as she keeps her wifely devotion, no karma attaches to her. The sages had stopped their wives from going to Krishna, but afterward how deeply they repented is told in the verses of the Bhagavat, Canto 10, Chapter 23, verses 42 to 52.

Among the sakhis (couplets) of the Naam-Rup-na-Mel, Maharaj Jivandasji wrote eight sakhis specifically concerning the sages' wives.

_Main Ajodha-men Jivana, man mero Gokul manhi. Rishi patnisu kol hai, so birad birasat nahin._ (331) (Says Jivan[das]: 'I was in Ayodhya, yet my mind stayed in Gokul, on when I would take birth there; because the promise I made to the sages' wives is a vow that is never forgotten.')

Sadguru Maharaj Jivandasji says that the Lord says: 'When I was in Ayodhya in my Ram incarnation, my mind remained fixed on Gokul, on when I would take birth there, because the promise I had given to the sages' wives — that in my Krishna incarnation I would accept them — is a commitment that is never forgotten.'

_Rishi patnisu Jivana, doodh bhaat liyo maag. Ek prem virahi bhai sundari, tan apno hi tyaag._ (332) (Says Jivan: 'From the sages' wives I asked for and took milk and rice; one beautiful woman, held back by her husband, gave up her own body in the pain of love's separation.')

Sadguru Maharaj Jivandasji says that Lord Krishna asked the sages' wives for milk and rice and took it from them; moreover, one beautiful woman, being held back by her husband, gave up her very body out of the pain of separation from love [for the Lord].

_Nari bandhi Jivana, sang apno hi jaay. Prem pritsu tan taji, jai doodh bhaat khilaay._ (333) (Says Jivan: 'The wife was bound while her own companions went on ahead; out of love she gave up her body, and went to feed [the Lord] milk and rice.')

Sadguru Maharaj Jivandasji says one sage had bound and held back his own wife; and since her companions were going on ahead, out of the intensity of her love she gave up her body, and her soul went to Shri Krishna and fed Him milk and rice.

_Bol bandh aage diyo, rishi patnisu hod. Taahi vachansun Jivana, men ye bandhi nari chhod._ (334) (Says Jivan: 'Earlier I bound myself by a vow to the sages' wives; to fulfil that word, I have set free this bound woman.')

Sadguru Maharaj Jivandasji says the Lord says: 'Earlier, in my Ram incarnation, I bound myself by a promise to the sages' wives to grant them loving devotion; to fulfil that vow, I set free this bound woman and gave her loving devotion, thereby completing my promise.'

_Purush nakaaro jo kare, to naar chede taahi jaay. Rishipatnisu Jivana, Raghupati bhaye sahaay._ (335) (Says Jivan: 'When the husband flatly refuses and holds his wife back, the Lord Himself came to that sage's wife's aid.')

Sadguru Maharaj Jivandasji says that whenever a sage's wife was flatly refused and held back by her husband, the Lord would in this way send for that woman and bring her to Himself — thus Lord Ram came to her aid.

_Rishipatnipe paahuna, Hari gaye Jivandas. Manvaanchhit phal poorke, puru abala aash._ (336) (Says Jivandas: 'The Lord went as a guest to the sages' wives, and fulfilled these women's heartfelt desires.')

Sadguru Maharaj Jivandasji says Lord Shri Krishna went to the sages' wives as a guest, and by granting them the fruit of the loving devotion their hearts desired, He fulfilled these women's longings.

_Paramapad paami premdaa, Harie kiyo haath bhojan. Vrindavanma Jivana, sakh gop kahe dhanya dhanya._ (337) (Says Jivan: 'The Lord ate food from the hands of these loving women, who attained the supreme state; the cowherds of Vrindavan called them blessed, blessed.')

Sadguru Maharaj Jivandasji says the Lord ate food made by the hands of these loving young women, and thus they attained the supreme state — the highest state of loving devotion — so that all the cowherds of Vrindavan began to call them blessed, blessed.

_Chhappan bhog pooran bhayo, paayo doodh aur bhaat. Krishnavatare Jivana, aaroge Raghunath._ (338) (Says Jivan: 'On receiving the milk and rice, the Lord felt as though He had partaken of the full fifty-six-course feast; in the Krishna incarnation Ram ate this food with love.')

Sadguru Maharaj Jivandasji says that on receiving the milk and rice offered by the devotees with love, the Lord felt the joy as if He had partaken of the full fifty-six-course feast (chhappan bhog). In the Krishna incarnation, Ram [the Lord] ate this food lovingly.

Citing the example of the sages' wives, the Samagam said that since a wife acts according to her husband's command, whatever karmic fault arises from the acts a man performs attaches to the man, not to the woman — even moral law (niti-niyam) says the same.

_Raagnyashchaamatyaja doshah patnidoshastu bhartari, tatha shishyarjitam paapam guruh praapnoti nishchitam._ (27) (The faults committed by a minister attach to the king, and the faults committed by a wife attach to the husband; in the same way, the sin earned by a disciple certainly comes to the guru.)

The faults committed by a minister attach to the king, and the faults committed by the wife attach to the husband; in the same way, sins committed by a disciple accrue to the guru. This is definitely established. The sages' wives, therefore, are without fault, because if a husband obstructs one's devotion, there is no fault even in leaving that husband — this rule applies to the sages' wives. And later, seeing their wives' good fortune, the sages themselves felt remorse.

In Kalyan, Year 30, Issue 4, page 86, there is an article by Hanumanprasad Poddar titled 'Four Essential Rules for Women.'

During a pilgrimage special-train journey, at one place a lady of a respectable family came to me and said: 'I wish to ask you one thing. I abstain from four things: (1) I do not eat a mahatma's leftover prasad; (2) I do not drink the water that has washed a mahatma's feet; (3) I do not touch a mahatma's feet; and (4) I do not put a garland or necklace on any man other than my husband. The sisters and brothers with me consider this a great fault and say, "You are committing a sin by this — your attention is on the body, you do not recognize the importance of the soul," and so on. Is this really a sin? Am I doing wrong by acting this way?'

I told this sister that all four of her practices are ideal and in accordance with scripture. There is no fault or sin whatsoever in them. Indeed, it is doing the opposite of these that can certainly be a fault or a sin. It is not proper for anyone to eat another man's or woman's leftover food, or to drink the water that has washed their feet. Such practices spread all sorts of disease and encourage immoral conduct; they give false and hypocritical people the opportunity to beguile simple, straightforward men and women and take improper advantage of them.

As for touching the feet and putting on a garland, mothers and sisters should adopt these four rules: (1) do not touch the feet of a man who is not your husband; (2) do not drink the foot-wash water of a man who is not your husband; (3) do not eat anyone's leftover food; and (4) do not put a garland around the neck of a man who is not your husband.

In Kotha district, the practice — following the custom of the acharyas there — of washing my feet and drinking the resulting water as charanamrit was being followed; I have had that practice, of taking my foot-wash water as charanamrit, stopped.

Also, in our community, for the past few years a practice has arisen of putting garlands on dead bodies. This practice is not necessary. And if there is a wish to garland the deceased, there is no fault in doing so; but the practice of garlanding is one that both men and women alike should give up. There is no fault in going to view a dead body.

In Vrindavan, the sages' wives fed Shri Krishna, and there is no fault of [associating with] another man in this, because the Lord is the Supreme Father, the husband of even the husband [the ultimate Husband of all]. These wives had not gone astray; a woman who wanders astray comes to ruin, as noted in the Hindu Book of Saints (with Bhagubhai in America), pages 14-15:

_Bhraman sampujyate raja, bhraman sampujyate dwijah, bhraman sampujyate yogi, stri bhramanti vinashyati._ (A king who wanders is honoured, a brahmin who wanders is honoured, a yogi is honoured for wandering, but a woman who wanders comes to ruin.)

A king who travels about is honoured, a saint who travels about is honoured, a yogi is honoured for travelling about — but a woman who wanders about comes to ruin.

_Vidya vanita veladi, ne rajani reet. Thaam kuthaam jue nahin, jo bandhani preet._ (Learning, a woman, a creeper, and the favour of a king — once attachment binds itself to them, they no longer look at whether the place is fitting or unfitting.)

In common everyday practice, once the inclination toward learning, a woman, a creeper (vine), or a king's favour takes hold and attachment forms, one no longer cares to consider whether the object is a suitable or unsuitable vessel for it.

_Nari nind mat kije, nari ratanki khaan. Jis khaan men paida hua, Dhruv Prahlad samaan._ (Do not disparage women; woman is a mine that produces gems — a mine from which gems such as Dhruv and Prahlad have been born.)

Do not slander women — woman is a mine that produces gems, a mine from which gems such as Dhruv and Prahlad have been born.

The Samagam gives great importance to the honouring of women. In the 80th verse, women are praised:

_Kulam pavitram janani krutartha vasundhara bhagyavati cha dhanya, swarge sthitaastat-vitaropi dhanya yeshaam kule vaishnav naam dheyam._ (80) (The lineage in which the name of Lord Vishnu is uttered is a pure lineage; its mother is fulfilled; the earth becomes fortunate through it; and its forefathers, dwelling in heaven, become blessed.)

The lineage in which the name of Lord Vishnu is taken is a pure lineage. Its mother is fulfilled (kritartha). Through it, the earth becomes fortunate. And its forefathers, dwelling in heaven, become blessed.

It is written in the commentary on Tulsidas's Ramayana:

_Aasphotayanti pitarah pranrutyanti pitamahah, vaishnavo nah kule jaatas sanah santaar vishyati._ (2) (The forefathers clap in joy, the grandsires dance: 'A Vaishnav has been born in our lineage; he will deliver us.')

Lord Sadashiv (Shiv) says: O Parvati, the lineage in which a virtuous worshipper of Shri Ramchandraji takes birth — that lineage is blessed. It is worthy of the world's worship, and it is pure.

In the commentary on the 80th verse, the Samagam states: Shukdevji said, 'O King Parikshit, the lineage in which even a single Vaishnav has arisen — its lineage is pure, its mother fulfilled; the earth flourishes with abundance because of it; and its forefathers attain liberation.'

To remove the fault ascribed to women (abala), the Samagam cites a couplet (sakhi) of Kabir:

_Kabir, naari narak na jaaysi, sab santanki baan. Jinki kunkhe Harijan base, so ratnaakarki khaan._ (Says Kabir: a woman will never go to hell — this is the teaching voiced by all the saints; for she in whose womb the Lord's devotees dwell is like the ocean that ripens gems, a mine producing the Lord's own people.)

Das Kabirji says women will never go to hell — this is a teaching that all the saints have voiced, because she in whose womb devotees of the Lord (Harijan) are born is like an ocean that ripens gems, a mine producing the Lord's devotees.

Having recited this sakhi, Jivandasji said that, on the strength of the proofs given above, he removed the accusation of untouchability that had been attached to women because of menstruation, and declared: 'I command that on Sama Pancham you shall prepare an offering (thal) of sweets weighing one and a quarter ser as prasad; by this the blemish of menstrual impurity shall be removed.'

Jivandasji further said that our compassionate Father cherishes everyone — that is, the merciful Lord holds love for all. If a soul (jiva) proceeds having set aside its ignorance, there is joy; that is, if the soul gives up the craving for worldly maya and walks the righteous path, its welfare (kalyan) results. There are eight kinds of karma.

In the section of the Samagam [containing] Kabir's sakhi 'woman is faultless, a woman will not go to hell,' Jivanji's 138th doha is then given — a doha of the Vaishnav:

_Naari to niradokh, Vishnu ugat jo upaje. Nahi to byaai bhoond, jangal jangal bhatakat phare._ (138) (A woman is indeed faultless if a devotee of Vishnu is born to her; if not, like a sow that has farrowed, she wanders from forest to forest.)

Maharaj Jivandasji says that if her son grows up to be a devotee of Vishnu, then no karmic fault of any kind attaches to that woman; but if he does not become a devotee of Vishnu, then that woman — like a sow that gives birth to her litter and then wanders through every forest and wilderness — is likewise considered to wander through the cycle of birth after giving birth, in a similarly wretched state.

The Panchatantra, in the chapter 'Labdhapranasham', states in verse 50 [the printed Sanskrit text here is corrupted at several points]:

_Vaasorvichotpannaam abhajat munir Matsyatanayaam, tatha jaato Vyaaso shatagunanivaasah kimaparam. Swayam vedaan vyasyat [unclear] Kuru vansha-prasavitaa sa evaabhut [unclear] Kuru-vansha-prasavitaa sa evaabhut shrimaan ahaha! vishamaa karma-gatayah._ (50)

Sage Parashar had union with Satyavati, the fish-born daughter conceived from the seed of Vasu (a particular deity/king); from that union Vyas was born, and he, though born in this manner, was the abode of hundreds of virtues. What more can be said — he was exceedingly radiant. Alas! The workings of karma are indeed very hard to fathom.

Woman has been held to be faultless. I have noted, in the diary entry list for Samvat 2052 under 'A.V.G.', a saying told to me in the words of Bhagat Parag Das Raghunath of Puniyad:

_Janani bicaari shun kare, patthar padiya pet. Kaan mandir kaan mahel, kaan chandan ghase ke mel._ (What can the poor mother do — a stone happened to be in her womb. From one such stone a temple is built, from another a palace; on one, sandalwood paste is ground, on another, filth is smeared.)

One stone becomes the material for a temple, another for a palace; on one, sandalwood is ground [as an offering]; on another, filth falls. In all this, what fault is it of the mother [quarry] that bore the stone?

Trikamdas Gordhandas Dhodawala writes, in his 1978 diary, page 30:

_Janani bichaari shun kare, shathno thayo sang. Vivek vani vaato kare, lajve maat-nu ang._ (What can the poor mother do — her son fell into the company of a scoundrel; talking as if with discernment, he disgraces his mother's own body/lineage.)

Because of association with a wicked companion, an unworthy son is produced — like father, like son — what fault is it of the mother in that? Such a son, without understanding what is good, behaves and speaks badly and thereby disgraces his mother's womb.

Trikamdas, in the diary of Samvat 2024, page 54, wrote nine sakhis about women:

_Naari-kun na nindie, naari ratanki khaan. Je kukhe jag Narmada, Dhruv Prahlad samaan._ (1) (Do not disparage woman; woman is a mine of gems — from her womb come gems as great as the river Narmada, and ones like Dhruv and Prahlad.)

_Ganga Jamna Narmada, nadi naarini jaat. Snaan kari sukhiya thata, nar naari parbhaat._ (2) (Ganga, Jamna, Narmada — these rivers belong to the feminine kind; bathing in them at dawn, men and women become happy.)

_Ahalya Tara Mandodari, Draupadi bahu pati naar. Chhataan sati sansaarma, kahe chhe shastra pokaar._ (3) (Ahalya, Tara, Mandodari, and Draupadi — a woman with many husbands — yet scripture proclaims aloud that they are counted as sati [chaste and virtuous] in this world.)

_Ahalya Draupadi Sita, Tara Mandodari tatha, panchakam smaret nityam maha-paataka-naashanam._ (13) (Ahalya, Draupadi, Sita, Tara, and Mandodari — whoever remembers these five daily, their great sins are destroyed.)

Ahalya, wife of sage Gautam; Draupadi, wife of the Pandavas; Mother Sita, wife of Lord Ramchandra; Tara, wife of the monkey-king Vali; and Mandodari, queen of King Ravan — whichever man or woman remembers the names of these five sati women daily, their great sins are destroyed.

_Niti niyamne nade nahi, jagma ko apradh. Patit narne naario, thai gayaan jagma saadh._ (4) (Nothing in the world can override the rule of right conduct; women have turned even fallen men into saints in this world.)

_Natkhat niti chhodine, karvi purushni sev. Sevaye chit shuddhi chhe, me niranjan dev._ (5) (Giving up willful ways, one should serve one's husband; through service the mind is purified — [thus one attains] the stainless Lord.)

_Dasatanthi dukh tale, dukh daridra sahu jaay. Parmeshwar male palakma, anubhaviyo bahu gaay._ (6) (Through humble servanthood, suffering is removed and all sorrow and poverty depart; God is met in an instant — the experienced ones sing much of this.)

_Vrinda vakhanaai jag gai, patit paavan thaay. Bhog chadhe Bhagvaanne, tyaan paheli poojaay._ (7) (Vrinda [the tulsi plant] became renowned throughout the world and purifies even the fallen; when an offering is made to God, she is worshipped first.)

_Pati viyoge gopio, dharti maanhi samaay. Gopi chandan shir chadhe, dhari lok harakhaay._ (8) (In separation from the Lord, the gopis merged into the earth; as gopichandan [the sacred clay], it is applied to the forehead, and people rejoice in wearing it.)

_Mahaan purushne man thaki, raakho namva nem. Avinaashi prabhu aapno, samajhi karvo prem._ (9) (Keep, from the heart, a resolve to bow to great souls; understand that your Lord is imperishable, and love Him accordingly.)

_Hath dai saamu na bolie, bolta karie vichaar. Vichaar karine vartataan, sukhi thaay apaar._ (10) (Do not answer back stubbornly; think before you speak. Acting with thoughtful consideration, one attains boundless happiness.)

_Maan martabo motaa tano, jaalavtaan sukh thaay. Samaj vagar saamaa thata, sarvaale pastaay._ (11) (Preserving the honour and standing of one's elders brings happiness; opposing them without understanding leads, in the end, to regret.)

_Halimali sampe rahi, vasataan mahaa sukh thaay. Khenchataan karva jataan, dahaada dukhma jaay._ (12) (Living together in harmony and unity brings great happiness; going about creating friction and conflict, one's days pass in sorrow.)

_Maathaa saathe kaan jadya, kaho kem judaa thaay. Hasi hasaavi chaalata, dukh deshaavar jaay._ (13) (The ear is fixed to the head — tell me, how can they ever be separated? Going about laughing and making others laugh, sorrow is banished to distant lands.)

_Samaji varte sukh chhe, swarg samun sansaar. Anubhav shabdne samajta, upaje sukh apaar._ (14) (There is happiness in acting with understanding — the world becomes like heaven itself; understanding the word of experience, boundless happiness arises.)

_Murakh mahaa dukh bhogve, samje nahi lavlesh. Adham dashaae din thai, bhajve bhavaiya vesh._ (15) (The fool suffers great sorrow, understanding not the least bit; falling into a degraded, wretched state, he plays the part of a mere folk-actor.)

_Vakkar vinu jivan bane, male na shabdama vesh. Jathar vathar jagma phare, vartanma bahu pol._ (16) (Life becomes without dignity when one's outward words do not match one's inner truth; such a person wanders about the world haphazardly, with much hollowness in their conduct.)

_Pal pakde te padmani, e kahevat jag maanhi. Pal chuke pastaay chhe, juthun maanso naahin._ (17) (She who seizes the moment is the padmini [the ideal woman] — this is a saying current in the world; one who lets the moment slip regrets it — do not think this untrue.)

_Sadyo bhane sukhi ghana, gophal godaa khaay. Samju jan sansaarma, anahad aanand paay._ (18) (Sadyo says many appear happy, but the negligent one suffers hard knocks; the person of understanding attains boundless joy in this world.)

_Paanimaan rahine sadaa, karvun magarsu vair. Vagar vichaare vartataan, jeevan thai jaay zer._ (19) (Living always in the water yet making an enemy of the crocodile — acting without thought turns one's life into poison.)

_Paanimaan meen jem rahe, te sam raho sansaar. Jalkamalvat vartataan, thai jaay vedo paar._ (20) (As the fish lives untouched in water, so live in this world; acting like the lotus leaf upon the water, one's boat is carried safely across.)

_Name game chhe sarvane, akadaai ukhadi janaay. Samji vichaari chaalataan, aanand mangal thaay._ (21) (Humility is pleasing to everyone; stiffness and pride show themselves as unbecoming and get uprooted; walking with understanding and thought brings joy and auspiciousness.)

_Aavkaari aagal vadhi, preme karvi sev. Sevaaye mevaa male, poojie samji dev._ (22) (Welcoming and moving forward, one should serve with love; through service one gains the fruit; worship God with understanding.)

_Dev nathi deshaavare, deh devmaan dev. Bole te beejo nathi, sant vachanne sev._ (23) (God is not to be found in some far-off land — within the body itself the divine dwells; the one who speaks truth is none other than that indwelling divine — serve the words of the saints.)

_Kakalaate pade kanasvun, utpaat ghanero thaay. Shaanti male nahi jeevne, kankaase din jaay._ (24) (Falling into quarrelling brings distress; great turmoil results; the soul finds no peace, and its days pass amid strife.)

There are four types of women — Padmini, Chitrini, Hastini, and Shankhini — and there are likewise four types of liberation (mukti).

Kabir, Jivanji and others have declared woman to be faultless. In the book named 'Anangrang' (registration no. 281, page 5), it is written that, in the science of rhetoric (alankar shastra), the word for women in the Vedas carries the sense of liberation (mukti). 'Nari' — 'na ari,' that which is not an enemy — hence 'nari' means mukti, because no one bears enmity toward liberation; thus the meaning of the word 'nari' should be understood as mukti. The being who merges and becomes one with Narayan, who dwells in the ocean of milk — that form of liberation is named Padmini, because Narayan is the very first of all and bears a lotus (padma) at his navel; therefore Padmini means sayujya mukti (liberation of complete union). (1)

Chitrini (a clever, beautiful, and virtuous woman) refers to the being who has attained samipya mukti (liberation of nearness to God) — such a being takes incarnation and performs deeds like those of God. The liberation that is wondrous (vichitravati, extraordinary) is Chitrini. (2)

The soul that attains a form like that of Vishnu, bearing the conch, disc, and so forth — that liberation is named Shankhini; thus Shankhini should be understood as sarupya mukti (liberation of having the same form as God). (3)

Those who go merely to the abode (lok) of Vishnu and so on — that liberation is named salokata (liberation of dwelling in the same realm); the one who has hands and feet [i.e., retains a form] is Hastini, for beings of this fourth type do not attain the formless (nirgun) state — they remain endowed with form, with hands, feet, and so on; hence, having hands, this is Hastini, that is, salokya mukti.

Description of the Form of the Padmini

_Praata rakta kuranga shaava-navana purnendu-tulyaanana, peeno truNga kuchaa shireesh mrudu laasya-lyaashanaa dakshinaa, kullaa bhoj sugandhi kaam saleelaa jajaavati maanini, shyaamaa kaapi suvarna pankaj neelaa devaadi poojaarataa._ (7) _Unnidraambuj kosh tulya madan chhatraa maraalashvanaa, tanvi hansavadhu-gatih suleelam vesham sadaa bibhrati, madhyam yaa peelavi trayaankitam asau shuklaambaraakaankshini, sugreevaa shubhanaasiketi gaditaa naaryuttamaa padmini._ (8)

A woman whose face is joy-giving like the full moon; whose eyes, though their corners are reddish, are shapely like a fawn's; whose breasts are full, firm, and well-formed; whose body is soft as a cotton flower; who eats little; who is clever and modest, who carries herself with great dignity; who is fair like a golden lotus — not truly dark, but appearing so on account of her youth; whose bodily fragrance is at once like that of a freshly blossomed lotus (7). One who is alert even in sleep; whose voice is soft like the bud of a lotus, like the sound of a koel bird; whose body is very delicate; whose gait is like that of a swan; whose nose is shapely like a conch, straight and well-formed; who is devoted to serving the Lord, the guru, and the saints — a woman possessing these characteristics is to be known as a Padmini (8).

In this way, the characteristics of women who are Chitrini, Shankhini, and Hastini have also been discussed, describing what good qualities of temperament and the like are found in such women; but a bad temperament would be called a personal flaw — the natural fault of womanhood should not be reckoned on account of menstruation, since the monthly flow is exactly the same in every woman. Yet ritualists (karmakandis) have insulted women by branding them as untouchable. At the time of menstruation, a woman has been portrayed as utterly base, as stated in the Rishi Panchami Vrat Katha (the story of the Rishi Panchami vow):

_Prathame-hani chandali, dwitiyo brahma-ghatini, truteeye rajaki prokta, chaturthe-hani shuddhati._ (37) (On the first day she is deemed a chandali [outcaste], on the second a brahma-ghatini [killer of a brahmin], on the third she is called a rajaki [washerwoman], and on the fourth day, after bathing, she becomes pure.)

When a woman menstruates, on the first day she is to be regarded as a chandali, on the second day she is called a brahma-ghatini, on the third day she is called a rajaki, and on the fourth day, after bathing, she becomes somewhat pure.

According to moral law it is right not to have intercourse with a menstruating woman, but it is not right to consider her base or to deem her untouchable. By natural law, just as fruit trees bear blossom before they bear fruit, so too an adult woman, on menstruating, is called pushpavati (flowering, one who has blossomed) — and flowers, after all, are offered to God. Therefore it is not right to consider a menstruating woman base. Kabir indeed has said:

_Kabir, dashodwaar narakke, nishadin bahe lalaay. Kahaan kahaan shuch raakhiye, Ram samar lolaay._ (Kabir says: from the ten gates of this hell-like body, filth continually flows day and night with eagerness — how much, and in how many places, can one keep oneself pure? Better, then, to eagerly remember and repeat the name of Ram.)

Just as with urine and stool, filth continuously issues, day and night, from all ten gates of the body. So how can we possibly keep all of them pure? Better, then, to begin taking the name of Ram with love instead.

In the Bijak, in Shabda 72 (99), it says:

_Chalahu kya tedho tedho tedho, dashahu dwaar narak bhari bade, tu gandhiko vedho._ (Why do you walk about so crookedly, so crookedly? All ten gates [of your body] are filled to overflowing with this hell — you yourself are a bundle of foul smell.)

This is addressed to those proud of their bodies: why, considering yourselves clean, pure and holy, do you go about harshly regarding others as low and impure, unjustly and deceitfully judging others as unworthy? You yourselves possess a body whose ten gates are filled with phlegm and the like — you yourselves are nothing but a storehouse of foul odours. You yourselves were born from just such a foul-smelling body — so why now practise this hypocrisy of declaring others untouchable and impure?

In 'Duniyaana Dharmo' (Religions of the World), registration no. 541, page 366, Dharekhan states that Prof. Abrahams, through experiments, established that during menstruation a highly poisonous toxin called menotoxin forms in a woman's body. In the Gujarat Samachar supplement dated 11.6.07 [2007], page 7, Hina Trivedi, writing about women's menstrual flow, states that women suffer unbearable pain before their period. In the 13th century, it was believed that a menstruating woman spreads poison from her body, and that a nursing infant would die [from it].

From 1550 down to the present day, a menstruating woman has had to stay in a separate room, and eat from separate utensils. Jews too would keep such a woman in a separate room for 12 days and not allow her into the temple. Parsi women, at such times, may look at the sun and moon but keep away from fire, and may not speak with men. A Hungarian woman, during her period, may not make pickles. In Europe and Germany, women during their menstrual flow may not touch perfume or flowers, nor dance; they stay away from worship; and it is believed that if such a woman cooks food for someone, that person's lifespan is shortened. Such beliefs of one kind or another exist, and will continue to exist, in countries throughout the world. The time when menstruation permanently ceases is called menopause.

In the Vinod Pustakalay collection, Fata (Puniyad), registration no. 311, pages 190-191, in the book named 'Suhagraat,' Malaviya writes: Among the Jews, ideas regarding a menstruating woman were extremely absurd and repugnant. Among the Parsis too — unthinking followers of old custom — a menstruating woman is regarded as thoroughly loathsome and contemptible: not only is she kept apart from household duties, she is even removed from the house itself and sent to live in the lower part of the building, in a separate place where firewood and lumber are kept. In the hills too, a menstruating woman is put out of the house; in cold weather she suffers greatly from having to stay outside. She is already in distress as it is, and on top of that this cruelty is inflicted on her.

The author expresses the view that cruelty like that inflicted on an untouchable ought not to be inflicted on her. But helpless human society has, to this day, been unable to remove this blemish. On pages 194-195 of 'Suhagraat,' the author expresses the expectation that the leaders of society will have this blemish removed: it is fitting that the religious teachers (dharmacharyas), just as they are reconsidering all the old customs and making the necessary changes in keeping with the pace of the times, should likewise consider the cruelty of this kind being inflicted on women.

On page 118 he writes: our religious teachers ought therefore to consider this matter seriously and soon give a firm ruling on it. Among Gujaratis, a menstruating woman is not treated as untouchable; she only refrains from cooking. This same custom holds among the Marar queens, [other] queens, and thakuranis (noblewomen) as well.

On 28.8.1927, Krishnakant Malaviya expressed the above distress. Discerning people understand the truth of the matter, yet to this day they remain unable to confront Brahmanical or orthodox custom — this is their helplessness. Such sensible people expect that if the religious teachers would carry out some campaign and remove the fault of untouchability, that would be well and good. But setting aside the untouchability imposed on women, the religious teachers have not even removed the stigma of untouchability that has been fastened onto people such as the Dhed and Bhangi [Dalit communities] — hence Islam is being propagated [and gaining converts] as a result. Once a Dhed becomes a Muslim, he can be touched. In this way they are turning India into Pakistan.

In Litiyu-15, page 6, Revered Yadunathji writes: I still recall the campaign for [reinstating] menstrual restrictions that Manilal (Bapalal of Vadnagar) had run in Moti Paal. Bhagat Ramji Gokul of Suryadhoda had gone to Paal; in his presence, Manilal Maharaj began telling everyone that we ought to observe menstrual restrictions again. He said to Ramji Gokul, 'Isn't that right?' — to which Ramjibhai replied, 'There is no need for Uda devotees to observe menstrual restrictions.' Embarrassed by this, Manilal said, 'Oh dear, my pillar has just come crashing down.' [Note: Manilal and others of this kind are, in every case, Brahmin ritualists — hence Brahmins feel obliged to impose menstrual restrictions.]

Once, in Samvat 2038, I went to the village of Mathi in Jagdish Kotha district. According to the custom there, upon reaching the village outskirts (bhagol) I sent word of my arrival to the family of the parathara [the designated host household], so that they might come and receive me. After nearly an hour had passed, another bhagat came and told me, 'Maharaj, it would do if we lodged you somewhere other than the parathara.' I said that would be fine. Then that bhagat said, 'There is a difficulty in going to the parathara — there is a childbirth-bed [a mother who has just delivered] there.' I then said, 'I will go to the parathara itself; ritual impurity (sutak) does not affect me — that affects the Maharaj of Sardarpur, not me.' In this way, the Brahmins of India can never be freed from regarding menstruation as a source of pollution. Let the Brahmins do as they will — but if the mahants who go about within the Uda devotee community bearing the title of religious guru have been unable to stop the blemishes current in that devotee community, that would be one thing; but it is shameful when, on the contrary, they strive to smuggle into the community a blemish from which the devotee community is otherwise free. Coming to Moti Paal and spreading such blemishes, such mahants commit a grave offence. Akha has said: 'He robs you of wealth yet does not remove your delusion — what kind of guru is that to abandon? May God grant such a one well-being.' Even the followers of the Kabir Panth bring shame to Kabir's own name — Kabir who himself said that one should not accept pilgrimage and vows.
